#4972. Amflow launches two powerful new electric bikes, including its first SUV-style e-bike

Amflow, the electric bicycle brand that burst onto the scene with some of the most powerful and lightweight electric mountain bikes on the market, is expanding its lineup with two major releases. The company has announced global availability of its new Amflow TL Carbon, while also bringing its removable-battery Amflow PR Carbon series to the US for the first time.

Both models are powered by the latest Avinox mid-drive motor systems, which have quickly earned a reputation for delivering impressive power in surprisingly compact packages.

The biggest departure from Amflow’s roots is the new TL Carbon, which takes the company’s high-performance mountain biking DNA and applies it to a more versatile SUV-style electric bike. While less common in the US (ironically), SUV-style e-bikes are essentially a hybrid electric bicycle designed to act as an all-in-one, “do-it-all” vehicle combining the rugged build and off-road capability of an electric mountain bike with the practical, everyday utility of a city or trekking bike.

Rather than focusing exclusively on technical trails and aggressive mountain biking, the TL Carbon is designed to handle everything from daily commuting to touring and off-road adventures. And with Avinox’s RS800 battery featuring 800Wh of capacity, it’s got plenty of energy on board for diverse adventures.

The full-suspension bike uses the Avinox M2 motor, delivering up to 125 Nm of torque, which should provide more than enough grunt for steep climbs, heavy loads, and just about anything else riders can throw at it.

Avinox e-bike drive systems are known for many things, but chief among them is the extremely high power and torque they offer, eclipsing most other mid-drive motor systems on the market.

Despite that power and versatility, the TL Carbon weighs as little as 22.6 kg (49.8 lb). It also boasts an impressive maximum total weight capacity of 200 kg (441 lb), including the bike itself, rider, and cargo carried on its front and rear racks.

That’s a compelling combination for riders who want the performance of a premium electric mountain bike but need something practical enough to replace a car for everyday trips.

And perhaps most surprisingly, the price isn’t completely outrageous. The Amflow TL Carbon starts at $3,899 in the US and €3,499 in Germany, positioning it competitively against premium European trekking and SUV-style e-bikes.

Meanwhile, American riders are finally getting access to the Amflow PR Carbon series, which had previously launched in other markets.

Unlike Amflow’s earlier electric mountain bikes, the PR series features a removable battery, addressing one of the biggest practical complaints about high-performance eMTBs with integrated batteries.

The new 800 Wh battery weighs just 4 kg (8.8 lb) and can be removed for convenient indoor charging or swapped for a fresh battery to extend a ride. That’s especially useful for riders who don’t have a convenient charging outlet near their bike storage area.

Amflow claims up to 158 km (98 miles) of range under ideal conditions, though that’s based on relatively gentle riding on flat pavement in Eco mode. Riders tackling technical trails with high assistance levels should expect considerably less. But any way you slice it, 800 Wh is a huge battery for eMTBs and should deliver plenty of range under most conditions.

The standard PR Carbon uses the Avinox M2 motor with up to 125 Nm of torque, while the higher-end PR Carbon Pro upgrades to the more powerful Avinox M2S motor, producing up to 150 Nm of torque.

In the US, the PR Carbon starts at $4,999, while the PR Carbon Pro commands $6,799. European pricing starts at €4,499 and €5,899, respectively, based on German pricing.

All three bikes are available beginning today through ⁠Amflow’s official website and its network of authorized dealers. In the US, both models generally arrive as Class 1 e-bikes (no throttle) with a top speed of 20 mph (32 km/h), though Amflow models can typically be unlocked to Class 3 performance with a top speed of 28 mph (45 km/h).

Amflow has been one of the more interesting brands to watch in the premium e-bike space, largely because of how aggressively it has pushed the boundaries of motor performance and bike weight.

But these latest releases show that the company is thinking beyond simply building increasingly powerful electric mountain bikes.

The TL Carbon is particularly interesting to me because it brings that impressive Avinox performance to a more practical platform. As someone who spends a minority of my riding time in the dirt, Amflow suddenly looks a lot more interesting to me, personally. Not everyone needs a dedicated eMTB, but plenty of riders would appreciate a lightweight, powerful, well-equipped electric bike that can handle both weekday commuting and weekend adventures.

And the PR Carbon’s removable battery is a welcome development, especially as the industry continues to recognize that convenience and serviceability matter just as much as outright performance.

With the Avinox ecosystem continuing to expand across more bike brands and categories, Amflow is also facing increasing competition from other manufacturers using the same impressive motors. That makes it all the more important for the brand to differentiate itself through thoughtful bike design, not just headline-grabbing power figures.

#4970. All aboard! Massachusetts is getting 10 new electric transit trains

The Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority (MBTA) board of directors voted unanimously Thursday to approve the purchase of a new generation of battery-powered public transit trains – and they can’t arrive soon enough.

“(MBTA) has, obviously, an immediate need for locomotives,” explains William Wolfgang, the MBTA’s senior director of vehicle engineering. The new machines will replace the oldest locomotives in the MBTA fleet, GP40s built more than 50 years ago and F40s that are well over 30 years old. In a presentation to the MTBA board, MTBA said 13 of the GP40s have, “exceeded their useful life,” while the F40s will reach the end of their life between 2029 and 2035.

The MBTA will put in an order for 20 Siemens-built “Charger” locomotives; 10 Tier 4 diesel-powered hybrid electric units and 10 dual-mode battery/catenary electric units – and, beyond trackside power for charging the batteries, there are other challenges presented by going electric, most notably using existing cab cars to control the battery-electric units. “We’re going to have to work with railroad operations, engineering, and the Brotherhood of [Locomotive Engineers and Trainmen] to try and determine the best way to handle that,” adds Wolfgang. “That will be an upcoming change order once we get into the design review process.”

The total bill comes out to $310.4 million. A combination of state and federal funding will pay for the order, including a recent $200 million transfer from the Massachusetts Department of Transportation.

The contract includes an option for additional locomotives, although details were not discussed during the meeting. Delivery of the new Siemens Charger trains is set to begin in 2029, with all 20 set to be in service by the end of 2030. Siemens has delivered 440 Charger model hybrid- and battery-electric locomotives globally at the time of this writing.

For daily wear, I love a pair of 100% cotton underwear, and this one is one of the comfiest pairs I’ve tested. But it’s important to remember that cotton isn’t always the best choice for working out, says fabric expert Cathy Rust. That’s because (while it is super breathable), once it gets wet, it doesn’t dry out as quickly as other materials. Though if you prioritize natural fabrics for your underwear, this is a great pick.

After testing dozens of pairs of underwear, the Amazon Essentials Cotton Bikini Brief Underwear is an affordable choice that doesn't slack on comfort. It's made from cotton and stretchy spandex, so it's extremely soft but also super moisture-wicking. Plus, I like that it has a bit of snap for light compression, but it's not too tight or clingy.

This underwear comes in either a six-pack or a 10-pack, so you get a mega bang for your buck, as the six-pack goes for under $15. It also comes in tons of assorted styles—and the color options are endless.

It’s a bikini-style underwear, so it offers more coverage than a thong, but I love it because I can have these on all day and forget I’m wearing them. They have a higher leg cut than normal, which helps avoid pinching or bunching, even while I’m moving around a lot. I also notice minimal lines under my clothing with this pair, but I wouldn’t quite say it’s invisible.

I've washed this underwear a ton of times and have never noticed any shrinking or a change in quality, which isn't always the case for affordable Amazon underwear. If you're looking for good quality, inexpensive underwear, this pair is it.

Of all the thongs I’ve tried, this pair from On Gossamer checks most of my boxes. It’s the most durable pair on this list thanks to a high amount of nylon in the fabric. Wash after wash, it feels brand new. And, for a synthetic option, it’s extremely soft and comfortable. Additionally, it comes in many different coverage options (think: brief, bikini, high cut, etc), is super stretchy without slacking on shape and compression, and it has a cotton gusset, which is essential for wicking away moisture.

This underwear has plenty of stretch—it can expand super wide but still snaps back for a snug, comfortable fit, thanks to the spandex in the fabric. It comes in sizes XS to XL, but the extra stretch means it can accommodate a bit beyond that, too.To make matters even better, it’s buttery soft, so it literally feels like you’re wearing nothing. And, it looks like that, too—I’ve worn this underwear under super tight compression leggings, and you can’t see any seams.I wear the Heavenly Stretch Thong for everything—from the gym to the office to running errands—because it’s seamless, lightweight, and moisture-wicking. Even when I get sweaty, it stays dry and comfortable, so I never have to worry about dampness or chafing. By the time I leave the gym, it’s usually dry and feels completely weightless. No need to adjust after burpees or squats—it stays put the entire time.I’d recommend going with your normal size for this panty. I tried a pair in a size down, and found that while it definitely fit, it was a bit tight around the hips. My one con? I wish it came in more color options besides just black and tan.Read more: Best Moisture-Wicking Underwear

Even though I’m a thong girl through and through, a bikini provides more coverage and comes in handy when you're lounging at home or during certain times of the month. And this one is a favorite of mine. With a touch of lace and tons of fun colors, it’s anything but grandma-y. Plus, it’s so soft and comfy, I actually want to wear it all day. I’ve even slept in it—it’s full coverage but feels buttery smooth and cozy.

This pair is made from Tencel modal, which is twice as soft as cotton. Compared to cotton, it’s smoother, more lightweight, and resistant to shrinking. And get this: It’s also super breathable, which is hard to find in panties that aren’t made from cotton.

It's sometimes hard to find comfortable bikini-style underwear that doesn't dig into the skin or move around because of the amount of fabric on the hips. This brief fits like a dream—it stays in place without riding up and has the perfect mid-rise cut. While I wouldn’t wear it with tight leggings, it’s seamless under jeans with no visible panty lines. Plus, since it doesn’t shift throughout the day, I never have to worry about adjusting it.

The sizing is also super inclusive with this underwear, as it ranges from XS to 4XL, so you can always find the right size. And don’t even get me started on the color range—there are more than 100 colors and patterns to choose from (though you won’t find them all under one Amazon listing).

Cotton underwear is great for wearing all day because it's a naturally breathable material, says gynecologist and Chief Medical Officer of Bonafide Health Dr. Alyssa Dweck, MS, MD, FACOG. This pair is made from 100% organic Supima cotton, which has longer fibers than regular cotton, making it feel extra soft and smooth against the skin. The fabric also includes a touch of spandex, which adds just the right amount of stretch. That’s why I love to wear it for walks, Pilates, and even high-impact workouts when I want to feel supported, secure, and ready to move.Plus, the material isn’t too thick. Combined with the smooth lace trim, this underwear is invisible under tight leggings and workout shorts. That’s a big win, since I find it difficult to avoid visible panty lines in styles that aren’t thongs.

And while thong and bikini styles tend to get a lot of love for workouts, the French Cut is one of the most underrated styles, IMO. Its high-leg cut makes it easy to move around in since the fabric doesn’t bunch at the hips or feel restrictive. That makes this pair great for all workouts. Plus, I love that the fit sits above the hips while still offering plenty of coverage. They’re also great for low-rise or super-short shorts when you need a pair of undies that won’t show while you’re on the move. The delicate lace trim detailing also adds a feminine touch, making them great for wearing outside the gym too.

Of all the moisture-wicking underwear I’ve tried, the Spanx Fit To You Thong checked all my boxes in terms of fit, materials, comfort, and sweat-fighting abilities. The nylon-based fabric is soft, breathable, and keeps me cool. It dries quickly, even after high-intensity workouts. By the time I leave the gym, I never have to worry about sweaty underwear if I’m running errands afterward.

It stays invisible under leggings, which can be hard to find in underwear, even in thongs. This pair has light compression for a smoothing effect, while the mid-rise style sits right at the waist without peeking over. There’s also no elastic band, so I never have to worry about an uncomfortable digging sensation.

The moisture-wicking cotton gusset stays in place during even my most intense workouts, offering full coverage without shifting or bunching up. I was skeptical about the “one size fits all” claim, but the stretch really impressed me—it hugs the body just right and prevents any VPLs (visible panty lines). The “one size plus” option is a great addition, making the fit more inclusive. However, I’ve noticed that many colors sell out quickly in the “one size fits all” option, while the “one size plus” tends to stay in stock longer.

I rarely go for full coverage undies, but I love this boybrief style from Aerie. It’s so comfortable and lightweight that I find myself reaching for it on a weekly basis. Normally, full-coverage styles like briefs and shorts dig in and are just…noticeably there all day, IYKWIM. Not this pair. The low rise on the hips helps with the barely-there feel, as does the thinner, super breathable construction.

I also love that this underwear is made primarily from cotton (with a bit of elastane for stretch), which helps with that softness and breathability. The material truly feels like butter on the skin. It feels less like full coverage underwear and more like a skimpy short, so I often wear it on its own with a t-shirt when I’m lounging at home. But it also works great under looser bottoms like basketball shorts, sweatpants, or baggy jeans. I wouldn’t wear it with leggings or anything form-fitting on the bottom, because it does cause VPL under tighter clothing.

When you’re on your period, you need underwear that keeps you dry and wicks away moisture. The Knix Super Leakproof Bikini does just that, absorbing up to eight teaspoons (!!) of blood, pee, or sweat. So if you bleed through your tampon, you’ve got a backup—without needing a pad.

Unlike other period underwear I've tested (which uses ugly, puffy padding to prevent leaking), Knix’s design is super discreet. That's because it uses a moisture-wicking nylon exterior with a cotton gusset that absorbs liquid. Some period underwear feels bulky and constricting, but this pair is so thin and comfortable, it’s like wearing nothing at all. The bonded edges also help prevent side leaks, making it great for overnight wear when you want extra protection without a tampon.

And while leakproof underwear might not sound glamorous, trust me—this pair is anything but bulky. The built-in moisture-wicking pad is so thin you barely notice it, even under sheer lace pants (I tested it at my birthday party!). Plus, it’s machine washable and seamless enough to wear under leggings. If you have a heavier flow, Knix offers thicker options, but this pair is perfect for light days or when you need extra backup.

Merino wool is one of the best materials to look for in a pair of workout underwear, and Branwyn's Essential Bikini is my favorite merino wool option. It dries out very quickly, even when I’m super sweaty. I love that I don’t have to worry about wearing these straight from the gym to brunch if I’m in a hurry.

Merino wool as a technical fabric is one of the few natural fibers that actually performs well in activewear. It comes from the coat of sheep and other animals, is naturally antimicrobial, and wicks away and absorbs sweat rather than letting it sit on the skin. If you run hot during your workouts, you can trust this pair of undies to dry quickly.

The nearly seamless construction also means no weird pinching or discomfort. The stretch (from the spandex in the fabric) means it moves in every direction without feeling restrictive. In fact, this is the most flexible underwear I’ve tested during my runs. Each piece is dyed in small batches, making every pair unique.

I’ve had a few of Skims’ Fits Everybody Dipped Front Thongs for years—it’s that good, I couldn’t just stop at one. Hands down, it’s the softest pair on this list. The On Gossamer thong is thinner and has more spandex, giving it a more compressive, workout-like feel. But this one is soft and stretchy without that snap, making it feel looser and more buttery. Despite its high polyester content, it has more of a cotton-like texture that’s super comfortable. I wouldn’t wear this underwear with tight leggings as it has a looser fit and it's not seamless, but this is my go-to underwear to wear with trousers, jeans, or sweats.

However, it’s still extremely breathable and quick drying, and kept us feeling cool and fresh during HIIT workouts. Unlike other thongs I own, this one never digs into my skin.This underwear also has a dipped front, which I prefer while wearing low-cut pants or crop tops. You never have to worry about it sticking up over your pants, as it doesn’t have a super high, thick band.The “Fits Everybody” line is my favorite that Skims offers, and there are so many different bras and underwear you can shop within this soft, stretchy line. There’s an Adaptive Thong, T-String Thong (another favorite of mine), and my go-to bra, the Fits Everybody Scoop Bralette.

In my opinion, every woman needs a good pair of boyshorts—for sleeping, extra coverage under short dresses, layering under jeans for warmth, or even wearing solo to yoga or Pilates. This pair from lululemon is perfect for all of that. It looks just like a pair of biker shorts (so no one will know it’s underwear!), but it has the breathability and moisture-wicking benefits of a great pair of undies.

This short is made from 91 percent modal (which is softer than cotton) and nine percent elastane for the perfect amount of stretch. It feels buttery soft, but the bit of spandex gives it a subtle snap, making it great for workouts or light compression under a dress. The flat seams stay invisible under clothes and help prevent chafing, while the smooth waistband sits comfortably without digging in or showing through.

This short has a five-inch inseam and a super high rise, making it a versatile fit for all kinds of outfits. In my opinion, it’s the perfect length for layering under clothes. When I wear it solo to a workout class, I wish it didn’t have stitching at the crotch—this makes it look more like underwear than workout shorts. But don’t get it twisted—I still wear it to the gym all the time. Plus, it’s moisture-wicking and quick drying, so I never have to worry about feeling damp down there after a sweaty sesh.

As a style writer, I test tons of underwear. For the original version of this story, written in 2023, I rounded up my all-time favorite pairs I’ve ever worn. Over the past three years, I’ve continued to put them through their paces (and tried even more options) to find only the best underwear for women.

In addition to speaking with fabric and feminine health experts about what to look for in a good pair of underwear, I tested each pair at the gym, around the house, on errand-running days, and on long days out and about to see which ones earned top marks across comfort, style, breathability, rise, fit, size options, and more. I wore and washed each pair multiple times, and rated them based on the following:

#4968. Climate shapes microbial nitrogen pump in forests, not in farmlands

Microbes build a long-lived nitrogen reservoir in soil from the remains of dead bacteria and fungi, which cling to minerals and resist decay. The microbial nitrogen pump turns nitrogen taken up by living microbes into this persistent pool, and microbial nitrogen use efficiency (NUE) has long been assumed to regulate this process.

#4967. In This Midcentury Nashville Home a Mosaic Rainbow-Hued Window Brings Color to the Earthy Interiors

Here’s one you may not have heard before: What do Serge Mouille sconces, a Louis Poulsen artichoke pendant, and Borge Mogensen dining chairs have in common? Hint, hint: They all live in the Nashville home of Doug and Carina Jenkins, the founders of antiques and vintage furniture store Eneby Home.

One might reasonably presume the home of antiques purveyors to be chock-full of one-of-a-kind finds from far-flung locales, and while that is certainly the case here, the husband-and-wife duo’s house otherwise expertly subverts expectations.

Built in 1970, the uber-quiet four-acre property sits at the top of a hill overlooking seemingly endless rolling valleys. It’s surrounded by native honeysuckle bushes and Tennessee Fieldstone, and the sun sets on the front side of the home at 6:37 p.m., says Doug, who dreamed of building what he describes as an “art gallery” for their furniture.

The Jenkinses kept the wall of original Tennessee Fieldstone—and the original copper fireplace—but added their own flair with vintage furnishings, like a La Mura sofa, Gianfranco Frattini for Cassina leather lounge chairs, a Charles Dudouyt credenza, and a 1960s marble fossil coffee table from Italy. “It’s super unique,” says Doug. “It doesn’t have a name behind it.”

Doug and Carina Jenkins, the founders of Eneby Home, with their daughters. They kept the original Tennessee Fieldstone on the wall and paired it with an antique marble dining table that’s “huge and heavy,” says Doug. “The guys hated bringing stuff to our house.” Even though the Louis Poulsen artichoke pendant is often seen in copper, the Jenkins were able to source one with a green finish, seen here. The chairs are Borge Mogensen; the 1960s geometric painting is from France.

A well-lit workspace features a vintage 1950s desk, an Italian cocoon lamp, and a Hans Wegner chair from Denmark.

“There’s not a lot of this type of house in Nashville,” says Greg Dutton, the founder and architect behind Columbus, Ohio-based and AD PRO Directory design firm Dutton Studio. “But we had to look past what was there—a mixed bag with a new era in each room—to create a backdrop for the work they do.”

Cue the blank slate. The couple bought the house as-is—black toilets, mustard-hued siding, and early 2000s kitchen included—and embarked on a “bigger than expected” renovation, says Doug, that translated to moving walls, updating floor plans, a new roof and flooring, and overall furnishings, of course.

With the resulting minimalist white walls and clean lines, how does one amass the amount of character evident here? “When you build in materials that have inherent imperfection, that naturally bakes in a lot of warmth,” says Dutton. Think locally sourced, character-grade white oak flooring throughout; imported reclaimed European bluestone that’s well over 100 years old in the primary bath; and an original copper fireplace in the living room.

“The mosaic supposedly came from a building in Bologna,” says Doug. “The morning sun comes up on this side” and ignites a fire of filtered light within the home.

“The island has a commercial look to it,” says Doug of the Vipp system. “It hit every box. It’s sick.” Dutton helped reconfigure the space’s floor plan to open the room to the dining area. The oven is by Miele.

A Guillerme et Chambron cabinet, sourced from Eneby Home, houses curiosities. The 1960s pendant light is Stilnovo.

The guest bathroom originally had a black toilet and smoked glass. Now it features vintage Serge Mouille sconces, of which Doug has “never seen another pair,” a 250-year-old antique Italian mirror from the 1800s, and a Josef Hoffman bench.

“Flaws make the house feel better, not worse,” says Dutton. “But creating something that looks effortless actually takes a lot of coordination. We wanted it to feel like it had just happened that way, and installing materials that feel like they’ve been there forever automatically gives the house permanence and ensures it’ll age gracefully over time.”

The push-and-pull between old and new, simple and full of character, clean and distressed is one the Jenkins family is familiar with. The balancing act makes the house interesting, says Doug, and the same inclination to lean on historic materials translates just as well to furnishings.

“Some of this stuff we’d been saving in hopes we’d one day be able to use it for our own house,” says Doug. One such example is a 1940s or ’50s-era, rainbow-hued mosaic window the couple bought five years ago and stored in a crate ever since. “We asked Greg to change the layout of the wall to make it work,” says Doug. The stone sculpture on display in front of the window is another; it’s 2,000 years old, from Rome.

An earthy palette in the primary bedroom lets the landscape through the windows do the talking. The sconces are by Biny; the oversized 1880 landscape painting is from France; the chairs are Borge Mogensen; the side table is Charles Dudouyt, and the floor lamp is La Borne.

“The fireplace is original, and we ran with it,” says Doug. “It’s New Mexico style and is super cool.” It’s paired with an abstract geometric art piece and a collection of vases from Denmark.

The stainless steel Vipp island in the kitchen, which the couple found in Denmark, is “the best thing in the house,” says Carina. “We moved from a house with a big pantry, and it was a challenge to figure out where everything would go. This island holds a lot.” Here, the family embraces the “European model” of compact living–albeit in 4,500 square feet. Dutton designed the black cabinetry wall as a backdrop for the island, which he calls a “piece of jewelry.”

Like any gallerist worth his salt, Doug spends five minutes each night turning off all of the ambient lighting in the house, like a pair of midcentury Biny sconces in the primary bedroom, an Orocolo lamp in the living room, and a 1970s Marika Carniti Bollea Nautilus lamp in the kitchen. Much of the light shines on a collection of artwork that’s so vast it’s often swapped out.

“We’ve already traded a few things,” says Doug. “If we find something we love, we want to use it. It’s what we do. It’s a perk, for sure.”

As is a home that’s forever. “Our girls want to come here when we’re old with their own kids,” says Carina. “They love it so much.”

The 1950s painting is from Denmark, the 1970s vase is from Sweden, the 1970s stool is Pierre Chapo, and the ceramic is from France. “We spend a lot of time in Denmark and like to mix Danish and Swedish,” says Doug. “We know a lot about that style of furniture.”

Dutton reworked the floor plan in the primary bathroom to set the vanity under a skylight. “We don’t use much overhead lighting,” says Carina.

#4965. The Best Gifts for Wives That She’ll Never Forget

To inspire you, we asked the wives on our team what gifts they wanted this year.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Finding the perfect gift for your wife is an opportunity to show her you really get her. I tapped my fellow Women’s Health editors, many of whom are wives and girlfriends, for an honest take on what they’d genuinely want from their partners. Trust me: these picks deliver. Whether she’s crushing workouts or leveling up her self-care routine, these gifts will make her feel celebrated and supported.

Even if you’re not currently searching for the perfect anniversary or birthday gift, there’s never a wrong time to surprise the woman you love with something thoughtful. For example, if your wife enjoys yoga, she’ll love Stakt’s folding mat. Or, maybe she’s serious about her morning rituals? In that case, she’ll love this five-minute journal to inspire some mindfulness first thing in the a.m. Perhaps she’s always got her eye on the latest wellness and recovery tools, making a pick from Therabody sure to please.

Below, find the best gift ideas for her in 2026. From fitness gifts to stress-relief gifts, this list is full of awesome tokens of appreciation for your better half.

Some sneakers are made to withstand all her tough workout sessions. Others are made to look good, and these cult-favorite Veja sneakers fall into the latter category. The casual sneaker is perfect for wearing to brunch, errands, and even work. Stylist Rose Lauture says these are a gift your wife will always want to wear. “It’s the best everyday sneaker to add to her wardrobe.”

If your wife is a reader, chances are she loves curling up with a good book before bedtime. What does she love less? The back pain that comes with trying to sit up comfortably against a headboard, using only her normal pillow for support. The solution: This WH top-selling backrest pillow. It’s made with a teardrop design (where one end is thicker than the other) that aligns the back for proper posture and provides extra lumbar support.

If your wife has a habit of unintentionally letting her coffee go cold before she’s able to drink it all, this Ember smart mug makes a great gift. It will lock in her ideal sipping temperature until the very last drop, keeping it warm all day while it’s on its charging coaster (only 90 minutes if it’s not). Your wife will appreciate just how much you care about perfecting her morning routine, even on the busiest weekdays.

This WH-bestselling fill-in-the-blank book is full of imaginative prompts that will inspire you to open up about what you love about your wife. The best part of this personalized gift? You can make it exactly what you want—fill it with cute romantic thoughts or naughty funny ones. She’ll thoroughly enjoy flipping through every page.

This bath bundle from Cozy Earth screams coastal serenity, and it will make her me-time that much better. “They have this really interesting woven texture that feels plush but also makes drying after the shower or bath really easy,” says lifestyle director Lindsay Geller, who’s obsessed with these towels. “I love the light blue color, especially because these towels don’t shed at all, so they always look brand new.” The bath bundle comes with two bath sheets, two bath towels, two hand towels, and four washcloths.

If she’s been complaining that her go-to exercise mat is starting to wear thin, the Stakt Mat makes an awesome replacement, and as a bonus, it’s probably more supportive than anything else she’s already got lying around. “It’s thicker than typical mats and folds rather than rolls, so it’s quick and comfortable to use for yoga, resistance training, and Pilates workouts,” says WH fitness contributor Talene Appleton. It’s especially great for those with tender knees, since it’s easier on the joints, she adds.

Wives on the go need headphones that can keep up. That’s just what this sporty option from Bose does without sacrificing any sound quality. They’re the perfect gift for the wife who regularly commutes to work and/or trains outdoors. Worth noting: They don’t go into her ears, allowing her to hear the world around her while still listening to her favorite playlist with crystal-clear clarity.

Pajamas should be effortlessly cozy without overlooking style. And that’s precisely what this set does. It's made with soft and stretchy jersey fabric that hardly wrinkles.

We can’t imagine a better evening for the ultra-competitive wife—especially if she loves true crime—than this immersive game. It’s a WH bestseller because players get to take on the role of detective and try to solve a murder mystery. With codes that need to be cracked and realistic motives that need analyzing, it’s like living out your own true crime podcast.

Give that ice pack she’s got in the freezer a tech-y upgrade. This portable recovery tool from Therabody, which is a brand beloved by WH readers, offers cold and heat therapy wherever she needs it. The palm-sized, wearable pad comes with three preset options—cold, hot, and a blend of both—that can be used to treat sore muscles or other pain, like period cramps.

Brand hype aside, there’s so much to like about this Dyson hair dryer. It’s a favorite among WH editors with different hair types, who all swear by it for a super-fast blowout with minimal heat. Our beauty editors say it’s worth every penny, especially since it comes with five attachments—a diffuser, a wide-tooth comb, a flyaway attachment, a styling concentrator, and a gentle air attachment. It’s a splurge, but a failsafe gift you can’t go wrong with.

Named the best budget option in our best sweatpants list, these sweats are for both lounging and getting movement in, even if it’s just running to catch her next flight. It’s designed with a cropped leg and relaxed fit, and of course, it’s stretchy and moisture-wicking, too.

The Everywhere Belt Bag is single-handedly keeping fanny packs in style, at least that’s the consensus among WH editors. The small bag is perfect for storing everyday essentials like keys, lip gloss, cell phones, and other small items. Even better, it’s always available in an endless array of cute colors and seasonal styles.

A weekend getaway is all the better with the right duffel—preferably one that meets your wife’s every packing need without weighing her (or your car) down. Enter Etronik. It has plenty of space for several days of ‘fits, a hidden shoe compartment, and a padded shoulder strap that makes it more comfy to carry. As a bonus, it’s easy to clean.

These cozy memory foam loafers are a low-key treat your wife will actually wear around the house and after workouts. The plush lining hugs her feet, and the cushy insole gives just the right support for lounging or light errands.

For some people, there’s no such thing as too many skin care gadgets. If that sounds familiar, gift accordingly with one of WH’s favorite facial wands. This tool utilizes four different functions to boost blood circulation and spark cell turnover that results in more glowy skin.

Go classic with these pink and red roses. Same-day delivery makes them a perfect last-minute save, and spares you a wait in the flower-shop line. Reliably romantic for her, and convenient for you.

This nylon tote is the definition of practical luxury. It’s roomy enough for a laptop, gym gear, or groceries, yet light and chic. Plus, it folds flat for travel, zips shut, wipes clean, and handles wear and tear (even editors who’ve washed the leather straps say it bounces back). For the wife who’s juggling life on the go, it’s a bag that works as hard as she does.

Sometimes you just want a pair of pillows for shoes, and as impossible as that seems, it’s not. These Oofos sandals really do make you feel like you’re walking on clouds. If your wife’s a runner, works on her feet, or regularly complains about being sore, she’ll love these shoes just as much as Accardi does. “My feet are always sore after pounding pavement, but these marshmallow-like slides are the perfect recovery shoes,” she says. “I wear them indoors and outdoors to help relieve my achy joints. Plus, they’re machine-washable!”

Whether she wants to use it to pick up those potato peels in a jiffy or for an easier way to clean the air vent, this portable vacuum from KitchenAid is a game changer. It comes with a rechargeable battery for cordless use and several attachments, including a crevice tool perfect for reaching hard-to-clean areas.

#4964. Do Your Muscles Need a ‘Creatine Washout?’ It Depends.

The benefits might be more mental than physical.

CREATINE IS THE prom king of social media—everyone’s talking about it. And not always nice things, either. Because for all the (very warranted) complements about how creatine can help you grow stronger, there’s also some (baseless) behind-the-back whispers about how it can make your hair fall out, poison you with heavy metals, and yes even kill you.

Between this polarization, there’s the seemingly reasonable personal stance of Andrew Huberman, PhD: Take creatine, but also take a creatine break.

Just in case you’re unfamiliar, a Huberman is a neuroscientist and associate professor in the Departments of Neurobiology and Ophthalmology at Stanford University School of Medicine. And he only hosts one of the most popular health podcasts of all time, Huberman Lab. When Huberman says anything about anything, people listen.

So when Huberman posted that he does a “creatine washout” every four months “just to see what effect it continues to have over time,” you have to wonder.

IT’S THE TIME period after you stop supplementing with creatine. The term is used frequently in scientific research that assesses the effects of creatine supplementation, often in athletic performance studies.

But, admittedly, there aren’t that many studies that look at the creatine washout phase itself. The most recent goes all the way back to 2004: “Effects of repeated creatine supplementation on muscle, plasma, and urine creative levels.”

In that study researchers found that levels of muscle phosphocreatine—that’s the amount of creatine stored within muscle cells—did not return to pre-supplementation baselines even after a 30-day washout period.

Since that 2004 study, there hasn’t been any supportive—or contradictory—science, but the lead author says the findings hold up more than 20 years later.

“Four to six weeks is a typical response and depends on dietary creatine, response to supplement, etc.,” says Eric Rawson, PhD, FACSM, Chair of the Department of Health, Nutrition, and Exercise Science at Messiah University, and a co-author of the 2004 washout study.

MAYBE, BUT NOT for reasons you might think.

“Questions about creatine washout and/or cycling supplementation are best handled from both physiological and behavioral perspectives,” says Rawson. “When I am asked about washout and cycling, I always ask people if they have similar concerns about their multivitamin. Or their calcium supplements. Or whey protein.”

Meaning, do you have the same washout concerns about creatine as you do your other supplements? Probably not.

“There appears to be a lingering concern about long-term creatine supplementation that is not supported by data.”

That said, Rawson says that some people, including many athletes, can feel overwhelmed by demands of maintaining their fitness edge—to the point where it’s good to take a break for mental health.

“Taking an off-season break from some of the usual routines, which includes, training, meal frequency, macro-nutrient intake goals, and the daily dietary supplement routine, can provide a break and perhaps some relief from the usual routine,” he says.

How long a break is sort of up to you and your long-term goals. But let your body and brain be the judge of that—not whatever you hear on social.

Paul Kita is a Deputy Editor at Men's Health, where he has covered food, cooking, nutrition, supplements, grooming, tech, travel, and fatherhood at the brand for more than 15 years. He is also the author of two Men's Health cookbooks, Guy Gourmet and A Man, A Pan, A Plan, and the winner of a James Beard Award.

#4962. Victorian Architecture Meets Mediterranean Charm in This Warm and Whimsical London Home

Interior designer Marta de la Rica describes herself as “a New Yorker by birth, French by adoption, and Spanish at heart.” That mix of cultures would prove to be an asset for one of her recent projects: the 5,382-square-foot four-story home of a family of four in London. A fine example of Victorian architecture, the building, located in the quiet residential neighborhood of Battersea and only steps away from Battersea Park, was built in 1879. “I already knew the clients, since I had previously designed their home in Bilbao, and I knew what kind of atmosphere the family wanted as well as what was particularly important to them about their home,” says de la Rica.

The walls of the stairwell are painted in Yel-01 Smooth by Clayworks and the Clam Shell Large light fixtures are by Porta Romana. The floor is made of several different marbles: Negro Marquina, Perlado, and Rojo Alicante.

The young family is originally from Spain but had already been living in London for nearly 10 years when they decided to buy a single-family home there. De la Rica decided to design spaces for them with a British-Mediterranean look that reflects the character of the historic Victorian architecture and the demands of modern family life. “The family wanted an elegant and peaceful home that, above all, would be warm and cozy,” says de la Rica. “For us, that meant creating spaces with comfort, character, and personality.”

Two midcentury armchairs sit in front of a Louis XIV fireplace from 1700.

Light brown and rust tones dominate the living room’s color palette.

Since the clients are Spanish, the project had a particularly interesting cultural dimension for the designer, as she explains: “We wanted the house to feel personal to them while also remaining true to its London identity and the Victorian architecture. So the project became a dialogue between English interior design and a more relaxed, Mediterranean lifestyle,” says de la Rica.

De la Rica’s interiors combine English interior design and a relaxed lifestyle in this Victorian building where the sunroom doubles as a dining room.

Originally, the family had been looking for a home in a different part of London, but when they saw this house, they were immediately taken with it and changed their plans. The building’s structure was in very good condition; only the floor plan needed to be reconfigured. “Above all, we wanted to preserve the spacious rooms, the ceiling heights, the bay windows, and the staircase,” explains the designer.

A relaxed breakfast setting with chairs by Vintola Studio and Benjamin pendant lights from Felix Lighting,

Visually, all the rooms have an almost opulent feel, yet at the same time, each one reflects its particular purpose. The ground floor includes a study, a living room, a kitchen, af amily room, and a sunroom, which also serves as the dining room. The parents’ bedroom is located on the second floor. A separate children’s area with bedrooms and play areas was created on the top floor. “The sunroom is a big part of the character of the house. To build the basement, it had to be demolished and rebuilt. It was very important to us to preserve the extraordinary presence of this space and its connection to the rest of the house,” says de la Rica.

The designer made the transitions from one room to the next as natural as possible by ensuring that the materials and atmosphere flow seamlessly.

The living spaces flow into the garden (designed by Matthew Wilson) and the terraces in front of the family room and the sunroom provide direct access to the outdoors. The garden features a pool, an outdoor kitchen, and a spacious dining area, providing additional spaces for social gatherings. The interior is characterized by elegant craftsmanship, custom details, warm colors, and high-quality materials. These choices highlight the grandeur of the historic home while also creating a cozy atmosphere.

A 20th-century dresser serves as a nightstand in the primary bedroom; an onyx lamp sits next to a vase filled with flowers.

“I particularly like that the rooms all have their own character, yet there is a clear, unifying design that carries throughout the house,” says the designer. It was also important to de la Rica to emphasize the scale of the house without having it feel cold or ostentatious. “Even in the larger rooms, there’s a coziness. It was very important to us to achieve this balance,” she says.

In the guest bathroom, the walls are painted in Yel-01 Smooth by Clayworks. Below the Negro Marquina marble sink by MDLR-Design, a curtain of Marly fabric by Colony.

The playroom showcases the Victorian architecture.

The children’s rooms are located under the mansard roof, which is typical of many Victorian houses in London. For the two youngest members of the family, the designer transformed the entire top floor with its sloped ceilings into colorful playrooms.

Amid dinosaurs and Mickey Mouse toys, the family’s son sleeps here. A Globe ceiling light hangs above the bed (Olofane).

De la Rica’s favorite parts of the house, however, are the living room and the dining room. For her, these are the areas where the home truly comes to life and where the design directly interacts with the family’s daily routine.

Above the large sofa in the family room, a Soren globe light from Pinch. The cream-colored Mayan Cuzco rug is from Bellbridge.

She particularly likes that the living room, dining room, and kitchen form a single, open space. “This part of the house allows for a very uncomplicated way of living,” she explains. “It’s very beautiful but not contrived or overly formal. It exudes coziness and spontaneity, and for me, that’s ultimately what makes a family home.”

For the walls in this bathroom, the designer chose Oli-03 Smooth by Clayworks, wall sconces by Vaughan, and a Calacatta Viola marble sink.

The wardrobe in the guest bedroom is upholstered with Ticking Stripe 1 Black fabric (Ian Mankin). The decorative Flax 03 tassels are from Samuel & Sons.

In the daughter’s bedroom, the rug is from Kvadrat. The closet doors are upholstered with fabrics from Yutes.

The Bert & May tiles in Garnet and Sand White were custom-made for this bathroom. The bathtub is Perlado marble.

This article originally appeared in the German edition of Architectural Digest.

#4961. Creatine Combo Supplements Can Be Confusing. Here's What an R.D. Wants You to Know

Creatine combo supplements are trending, but are they better than regular creatine? An R.D. breaks down the hype.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

If there’s one supplement I won’t stop talking about as both a dietitian and a consumer, it’s creatine. And while creatine has long been a staple in pre-workout supplements, now you’ll find it in everything from collagen supplements to greens powders to electrolyte mixes. Usually called creatine combo or creatine plus supplements, you’ll also find plenty of influencers raving about them right now. But are they actually any good and worth taking?

Creatine has earned the well-deserved hype as one of the safest, best-researched supplements for improving exercise performance, according to the International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN). When paired with resistance training, creatine can also support muscle growth, so I get the appeal of creatine combo supplements. Instead of mixing several powders and remembering multiple supplements, you can get creatine alongside other ingredients you already take. And fewer supplement tubs cluttering your pantry? Even better.

A creatine-and-collagen powder could be a good fit if you already take both supplements, while an electrolyte blend with creatine might make sense if you regularly use a hydration mix. Greens powders and post-workout supplements are other options, depending on your routine and goals. The catch? Not every combination provides enough creatine to replace a stand-alone supplement.

Creatine combo supplements can absolutely be worth trying, especially if they simplify your routine. But convenience alone doesn’t make a product a good buy. At the bottom of this story, you’ll find some recommended creatine combo supplements and pertinent info on them, plus lots more info about what to look for when adding one to your supplement stack.

According to the ISSN, 3 to 5 grams of creatine monohydrate daily is a well-researched dose for improving strength and exercise performance in most healthy adults, and creatine monohydrate is the most extensively studied form.

Some combination supplements provide less than that amount, so check the Supplement Facts label rather than assuming you’re getting an effective dose. For instance, Vital Proteins Advanced Collagen Peptides + Creatine provides 10 grams of collagen and 5 grams of creatine, meeting the recommended creatine dose. However, Ancient Nutrition’s blend lists 5.5 grams total of creatine and collagen on its Supplement Facts label, without breaking down how much of each you’re getting.

Higher creatine doses are also being studied for potential brain benefits. A 2025 study explored 10 grams daily, but there’s no established dose for cognitive health yet. If brain benefits are your goal, a stand-alone creatine monohydrate powder may be more cost-effective and easier to dose.

Creatine’s benefits depend on consistent use, even on days you don’t exercise. That’s because creatine works by gradually increasing and maintaining creatine stores in your muscles, not by providing an immediate boost after a single serving.

So, think about how a combo supplement would fit into your daily routine. A collagen powder containing creatine that you stir into your coffee every morning might make it easy to stick with.

Just because a product contains several popular ingredients doesn’t mean it provides useful amounts of each. Check the doses, whether those ingredients fit your goals, and whether you’re paying for anything you don’t really need.

A creatine-and-electrolyte mix may be worth the spend if you need both. But if you rarely sweat heavily or already get enough electrolytes through food and drinks, you might be paying extra for something you don’t need.

The same goes for pre-workouts. I’ve seen plenty of products with impressive-looking ingredient lists that provide less than the amounts typically studied.

Lastly, compare the cost per serving with buying creatine and the other supplements separately. For perspective, one study found that plain creatine monohydrate products cost an average of just $0.60 per 5-gram serving. By comparison, Vital Proteins Advanced Collagen Peptides + Creatine costs about $1.39 per serving. Sometimes the added ingredients and convenience are worth the extra cost. Other times, plain creatine monohydrate is the better deal.

My final take? If a combo provides a full dose of creatine monohydrate, includes other ingredients you’ll use daily, and fits your budget, go for it! Otherwise, I’d keep it simple: plain creatine monohydrate is affordable, effective, and easy to add to just about any routine.

#4958. ‘I’m Entering My Third Bodybuilding Competition at 52. Here’s How I Build Muscle in Midlife.’

“Strength, resilience, and the courage to pursue goals don’t have an age limit.”

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

When I was 20 years old, I thought I’d reached the peak of my fitness journey: I became one of India’s first female bodybuilders, and was even acknowledged in India’s national and world records book. It was an incredible honor, and I took immense pride in the discipline, strength, and athleticism it took to get there. Little did I know, though, that some of my greatest fitness accomplishments would come decades later, in my 40s and 50s.

Growing up, I always loved playing sports recreationally, and that passion for movement and competition eventually led me to bodybuilding. But at 24, I got married and moved to the United States with my husband; shortly after, I gave birth to my daughter at 29. With all these big life changes, fitness fell by the wayside. My life was centered around giving to my family, and somewhere along the way, I stopped prioritizing myself. Over the next two years, I became chronically exhausted, lost muscle, gained weight, and didn’t feel like myself physically or mentally.

Then, when I was 33, I decided to make a change. I thought back to the discipline and structure I once had with fitness and realized how much I missed that part of my life. I wanted to get back to those habits and rebuild the strength I once worked so hard for, so, I began making time for fitness.

My husband started watching our daughter after work while I began doing full-body workouts using light weights, focusing on consistency rather than intensity. I already had a strong foundation in strength training from my bodybuilding days, so I created most of my own workouts. But I also reached out to my former coach in India, who helped program some of them.

At first, the workouts were hard, and I was sore every day. But mentally and emotionally, I felt amazing; for the first time in years, I was committed to doing something just for myself. Starting then, I promised myself that I would never stop prioritizing my health again.

Over the next year, I worked my way up to hour-long workouts and continued lifting heavier weights. As a result, I gained significant muscle and lost more than 20 pounds. But the physical changes were only part of the transformation—I had more energy during the day, slept better at night, and felt more confident and comfortable in my own skin. Every workout reminded me that I was getting stronger not just physically, but mentally and emotionally, too.

As the years went on, I kept growing muscle and losing weight by strength training four to five days a week. Still, there was always a voice in the back of my head telling me to try bodybuilding again. So, at 48, I entered another competition. I worked with a coach who helped me gradually push my limits by lifting heavier weights, adding more challenging strength-training exercises, and increasing the reps and sets of my workouts. I also followed a strict plant-based, protein-forward diet (I became vegan for ethical reasons when I was 38). So, I ate lots of tofu, tempeh, lentils, beans, fruits, vegetables, whole grains, nuts, and seeds. The work was demanding, but it was incredibly motivating to watch my body transform through discipline and consistency.

Stepping back on stage again was a deeply rewarding experience, and I felt so proud of the hard work and dedication it took to get there. Most importantly, it was so empowering to show my teenage daughter that strength, resilience, and the courage to pursue goals don’t have an age limit.

I took four years off of bodybuilding since life got busy and I wanted to give my body a break from competition prep. But about a year and a half ago, I decided I wanted to challenge myself again and see what I could accomplish in this new decade of my life. My training approach didn’t change too much since the last competition—I just kept building as much muscle as possible.

In April 2025, I began my “bulk” phase, a period focused on growing muscle by increasing my calorie intake and lifting heavy. I followed a structured workout plan with a coach five days a week through two lower-body days and three upper-body days. During each session, I usually did five to seven exercises, typically for four sets of six to eight reps with heavy weight for muscle growth. I used a mix of free weights and weight machines, and some of my staple moves were pull-ups, leg presses, leg extensions, squats, lunges, chest flies, and lat pulldowns. I also intentionally incorporated pauses at the top or bottom of certain movements to make each exercise more challenging.

Training for a bodybuilding competition also means entering a “cut” phase, which involves reducing body fat so muscle definition can show on stage. So, in January of this year, I reduced my calorie intake while continuing to strength train with heavy weights. After my strength-training sessions, I also did 45 to 50 minutes of cardio on the stair stepper or elliptical. Additionally, I finished every workout with a core circuit to improve muscle definition that includes moves like hanging leg raises, situps, and bicycle crunches.

Recovery has always been non-negotiable for my workouts, too. I lightly stretched after every session, and on my off days, spent at least an hour doing deeper stretching with resistance bands and a foam roller to maintain mobility and reduce my risk of injury.

I swear by this protein powder to support my training and recovery. It’s easy to mix and has a smooth texture without the chalky taste.

These Puma sneakers are my go-to for lifting because they provide a stable, supportive base that helps with balance and even weight distribution.

I love this tofu as an easy way to get more protein. It’s delicious and the taste blends well into nearly any meal, from stir-fries to bowls.

I’ve learned that strength isn’t just about what happens in the gym. Every little habit works together as a system: how I train, eat, recover, sleep, and take care of myself mentally and emotionally. When those pieces are in balance, I have more energy, feel stronger, and perform better.

But instead of trying to change every one of my habits overnight, I took small, manageable steps, like dedicating just 20 minutes to myself at the gym. Once that became routine, I built on it by focusing more on nutrition and recovery, then eventually, I set my sights on returning to the bodybuilding stage. When I treat my body and mind as a whole, I’m able to gain strength sustainably, which allows me to keep doing what I love.

The simpler my workouts are, the more consistent I can stay with them. That’s why my coach and I work on foundational exercises like squats, lunges, presses, rows, and pull-ups. But to continue challenging my muscles in different ways, we use simple adjustments like tempo, pauses, and stance variations.

For example, while doing a squat, keeping my toes pointed forward targets my quads and center glutes. But turning my toes slightly outward helps me feel more activation in the outer glutes and inner thighs. Small adjustments like these allow me to keep progressing with simple and effective movements without constantly reinventing my routine.

For years, I was so focused on caring for my family that I stopped making time for myself. Getting back into strength training changed that. I realized that taking care of my health isn’t selfish—it’s necessary, and making that commitment has given me more strength, energy, and confidence in every part of my life. By scheduling my workouts like any other important commitment, planning ahead, and staying consistent even when life gets busy, I’ve found a way to prioritize myself while still being there for my family.

Today, strength training is about more than building muscle or preparing for a competition. It’s one of the ways I continue to invest in my health, challenge myself, and pursue goals that bring me joy. I’ve learned that you don’t have to be where you once were to start again. You just have to decide that you’re worth the time and effort, take the first step, and keep showing up.

#4956. Inside the Underground Mosques of Kazakhstan’s Surreal Mangystau Desert

Up until about 20 years ago, a faint trail up a steep hill through limestone-and-chalk cliffs was the only way to reach Beket-Ata, one of the sacred underground mosques—as they’re colloquially known—of Kazakhstan’s Mangystau desert. “There was no proper path then, but people made the difficult climb in the heat and wind,” my guide, Yerzhan Nagmanov, tells me as we embark on our way to the holy site—eased slightly by the stairs now carved into the stone. That arduous journey, the travelers believed, “was part of the pilgrimage.”

En route to Beket-Ata with Mangystau Tour 999, visitors walk a trail cutting through the steep hill.

The trail of stairs descending into the canyon en route to Beket-Ata.

As inhospitable as the roughly 64,000-square-mile desert may seem, it has attracted scores of people over the years arriving to see Beket-Ata and the four other sacred complexes scattered across its expanse: Shopan-Ata, Karaman-Ata, Shakpak-Ata and Sultan-Epe. Traveling between the five holy sites, the distinction between architecture and geology evaporates into the desert heat: Walls, ceilings, and floors are all variations of the rock from which the mosques were excavated. For pilgrims, the journey to these sacred sites is an act of devotion, where people come to honor revered Sufi masters, pray for blessings, and seek spiritual guidance in times of difficulty.

The mosques are hundreds of years old, collectively dating between the 12th and 18th centuries, but they’re new to the UNESCO World Heritage List as of this summer. The “Rock Mosques and Associated Sacred Sites of Mangystau” were added to the esteemed collection of landmarks in July.

Each mosque is associated with a different spiritual master within Sufism, the mystical branch of Islam. The five Sufi masters’ influence shaped the region’s religious landscape, and then the landscape itself, as all of the mosques—crafted in a rock-cut style that grew out of nomadic building traditions—seem to grow directly from the desert terrain; they’re carved into caves, tucked along the contours of cliffs and hillsides, and tunneled below the ground.

After three weeks travelling through Kazakhstan’s cities, mountains, and pine forests, I spent my final week in Mangystau, a landscape so different from anything I’d seen so far in the country that it felt like a whole world unto itself. Having recently visited Astana’s Grand Mosque, with its blue domes, soaring minarets, and gleaming expanses of marble, I wondered whether Mangystau’s rock-cut shrines might fall flat by comparison. For me, however, their lack of splashy grandeur is precisely what made them so compelling.

A stately arch welcomes travelers to the steps leading to Beket-Ata.

While I am not Muslim, I was fascinated by how the Sufi masters traversed this unforgiving terrain along with their families. Some walked hundreds of kilometers to establish places of worship far from the comforts of the world, spending years in prayer and contemplation before eventually being buried here. I was drawn to the way the rock mosques embody a humble yet stunning expression of faith shaped by the austere landscape, where instead of gilded shrines or massive palaces, devotion found a more organic form. Through guided 4x4 tours with Red Maya Travel and Mangystau Tour 999, I visited all five.

A necropolis inside the Shopan-Ata complex.

My first stop on the tour is Shopan-Ata, named after the 12th-century Sufi teacher. The complex consists of a vast necropolis (a large burial ground with tombs of religious figures and generations of pilgrims) of more than 2,000 monuments, including domed mausoleums and kulpytas, which are ornately carved stone steles traditionally used as Kazakh gravestones. The 12-chamber mosque is carved into the rock, and a shaft of daylight is cast onto two sacred wooden poles below. According to a local tradition, pilgrims recite a prayer and circle the poles three times counterclockwise, which is believed to help the spirits hear them. Visitors also tie strips of white cloth around the poles, the knot symbolically binding a prayer to the sacred site. These practices likely come from Shamanic and Tengrian traditions of tying strips of cloth to sacred trees and mountain passes to honor nature spirits––customs that became intertwined with local forms of Muslim saint veneration over time.

Nearby, a well offers pilgrims a much-needed respite; these sacred complexes grew around the few natural resources that made life in the desert possible.

Domed mausoleums at the Shopan-Ata necropolis.

The entrance to Shopan-Ata, shaded by a mulberry tree. These mosques were built around oases that sustained life in the harsh desert climate.

Legend holds that centuries later, Shopan-Ata appeared to Beket-Ata in a dream, offering spiritual guidance, making this shrine an important stop before continuing to Beket-Ata. Nearby, a well offers pilgrims a much-needed respite, its water an incongruous presence in a landscape this dry––a reminder that these sacred complexes grew around the few natural resources that made life in the desert possible.

The sacred wooden pole, around which visitors tie white cloth to seek blessings.

The final few stairs leading up to the Beket-Ata shrine.

Just over an hour away, Beket-Ata is perhaps the best-known of the five mosques. Founded by the 18th-century Sufi teacher Beket Myrzagululy, the shrine lies in a remote canyon about 170 miles from Aktau, the Caspian-side gateway to Mangystau. The steep descent into the canyon is a reminder that the effort needed to reach these shrines has always been a part of the devotion.

The structure is carved into the pale rock, its interconnected chambers following the curves of the cliff. Narrow openings in the ceilings pull shafts of daylight into the cool, dim rooms, where rugs are spread across the stone floor.

Communal dining is integral to Kazakh culture.

An imam is usually on hand to receive visitors and share information about the site. As we settle on the carpets, he details each of the chambers, one of which contains Beket-Ata’s grave, and another is associated with his sister. The remaining rooms are used for prayer, with separate spaces for men and women.

My pilgrimage continues into the dining hall, where a long, continually replenished table runs through the room, with pilgrims sitting on either side and eating together. The mosque provides some freshly cooked meat free of charge, while visitors leave bread, sweets, tea, yogurt, jam and other provisions for those who arrive after them—an especially vivid expression of Central Asian hospitality.

Next we drive across remote country to the Tyub-Karagan Peninsula for Shakpak-Ata, whose cruciform mosque is carved into a massive chalk cliff. Its porous white surface, which looks almost like honeycomb against the desert, was shaped millions of years ago when this part of Mangystau lay beneath the ancient Tethys Sea. Inside, drawings and inscriptions in Arabic, Persian, and Turkic—some dating back to the 18th century—offer a tangible record of the pilgrims who traveled here from across Central Asia, long before air-conditioned 4x4s and Starlink internet made traversing this unforgiving landscape simpler.

A honeycomb-like pattern along the rock face of Shakpak-Ata.

Slightly west, Sultan-Epe lies beside a deep canyon, where a stream threads through thickets of mulberry, buckthorn, blackberry, and wild herbs—another improbable pocket of green in one of Kazakhstan’s driest regions. Sultan-Epe is revered as a protector of seafarers and fishermen—a fitting association for a shrine overlooking the Caspian. According to local tradition, Sultan-Epe was the son of Hakim-Ata, a renowned Sufi poet and disciple of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi, which connects the shrine to the spiritual tradition associated with Shopan-Ata and, through his later spiritual mentor, Beket-Ata.

The stacked-stone entrance to Sultan-Epe.

The final stop on the circuit is Karaman-Ata, where a seven-hectare necropolis stretches across a low, open plot of desert dotted with funerary monuments, some more than 1,000 years old. The mosque is carved into the slope of a small marl hill, and as you descend into the rock, the temperature drops noticeably from the heat outside. A narrow passage leads to a circular room believed to be associated with Sufi rituals including devotional whirling, a type of worship that is expressed through physical movement.

Karaman-Ata, the largest of the five rock mosques of Kazhakstan’s Mangystau desert.

Reaching each site still means long drives across remote terrain, with limited to no mobile coverage or fuel services–making a sturdy vehicle and a trusted local guide essential. But after days spent traveling the region, these places begin to alter your sense of the desert. Around a well, beneath a mulberry tree, or at a table crowded with food and strangers, the landscape that seemed so stark and inhospitable reveals an unexpected generosity, preserved in the rituals of those who continue to make the journey here.

#4955. Range Energy shows how its eTrailer saves almost as much as a Tesla Semi

Range Energy, a company working to electrify trucking through the use of a trailer with its own battery and motors, has published an analysis showing how much fleets can save through electrification – and just at the right time, with diesel at record highs.

You may have heard a little something about diesel prices lately, which have just about doubled in less than a year due to Donald Trump’s war of choice in Iran.

Diesel is now at record highs, and it’s devastating fleets and truck drivers and anyone who uses any products that are delivered on trucks (so, everyone). It’s an urgent problem that needs an urgent solution, and solutions are not forthcoming from the responsible entities.

So, fleets have to seek another solution, and Range Energy would like to be the one that provides it.

Range is a startup based in California, founded and staffed by former Tesla employees and others from around the EV industry. It’s building an electrified trailer which we demoed at ACT Expo in 2024 (really, watch it, it’s a very cool demo) which promises to cut fleet fuel use significantly.

It does this by having its own battery and motors inside the trailer, meaning the tractor doesn’t have to work nearly as hard as the trailer can effectively pull its own weight. Even though the tractor still runs on diesel, it uses a whole lot less of it.

This differs from the other popular option for fleets: full electrification. There are a number of electric semi tractors available, and fleets have been moving to install them, getting their depots ready for charging. But Range lets you bring your own tractor, and electrifies the trailer instead.

Range previously published some early findings, showing a 36% reduction in fuel use in a testing scenario. It also did a pilot program with an egg farm in California, which improved the fuel efficiency of the farm’s diesel fleet by 50-70%.

Now Range has published its own white paper showing comparative savings that fleets can achieve with either its own solution, the eTrailer, or Tesla’s solution, the fully electric Tesla Semi. The paper does not cover the various other electric semi tractors available on the market today, just a face-off between Range and Tesla.

The analysis goes through several scenarios, mostly focusing on refrigerated trailer units (“reefers”), which is the first product Range is focusing on.

Trailer electrification is a great idea for reefers, because they usually fill up on volume rather than weight (called “cubing out”), meaning battery weight doesn’t eat into maximum trailer payload. Batteries also offer power to run refrigeration, meaning you don’t need to have a diesel generator on the trailer.

The upshot of the whole thing is that: fleets can save money with the Range eTrailer, and can theoretically save more money with the Tesla Semi, but the numbers are relatively close in the most common scenario, and the Tesla scenarios have a much wider spread depending on what implementation you consider.

For example, if you only use public chargers rather than your own depot, the Tesla Semi will be more costly because energy will be more expensive to your fleet than if you bought it at commercial utility rates. So, even though installing chargers in your depot sounds expensive, it will pencil out better in the end.

The best money savings came from having two Semis share the same charger, but that requires tight timings and overnight driving.

Another important feature Range points out is build time for a project. The nice thing about the eTrailer is it can slot into fleets immediately with little operational change required, whereas the larger charging needs of an electric tractor) tend to require bigger projects to get a depot ready with chargers (but despite the higher upfront costs, you get better long-term savings, since you avoid diesel entirely with an electric tractor).

In the end, Range found that its solution saves a little more money than the Tesla Semi does in most scenarios, but the difference is quite narrow, with each option having its strengths and weaknesses. Both solutions are better than diesel in most scenarios, but not all of them.

You don’t necessarily need to choose between the two, as an electrified trailer can still be used with an electric tractor. It works the same way in either case – using its own motors to take some of the effort off the tractor. This means extended range, for longer hauls with light loads that couldn’t quite make it on the Tesla Semi’s inherent range. And the benefit of being able to run the reefer while disconnected from the tractor or shore power remains as well.

The analysis has plenty of limitations. It has to estimate future diesel costs (it used a number below current prices, but still historically high), didn’t cover financing costs, it doesn’t have real-world data for the Tesla Semi, didn’t cover electrified tractor or trailer options from other companies, can’t analyze individual charging costs site-to-site since each is specific to a utility company, didn’t cover the myriad incentives available in various regions, and most of all it didn’t consider diesel emissions, which are a huge societal cost to everyone that electrification reduces (and full electrification reduces more).

So in the end, every fleet has a different use case, and should run the numbers themselves to see how either solution would fit in. But in the generalized case, it looks like there are plenty of savings available out there, whether through tractor or trailer electrification.

A good idea in theory but there are three trailers for every tractor-cab because trailers spend a lot of time sitting idle. For specific closed-loop customers and routes this can very very helpful but not as a general solution.

You know what can offer relief right now? Importing Class 8 Trucks. China is selling 280,000 heavy duty EV trucks this year. Trade barriers hurt economies.

Unfortunately, given diesel prices are at record highs right now, both of the options in the paper are a little suboptimal. Tesla Semis have been on order for almost ten years now, and Tesla only just claimed it has started production in earnest. And Range is still about a year out from volume production of its eTrailer, which it says will start in late 2027 – so, while an eTrailer will be able to slot into a fleet immediately when it’s available, it’s not available yet, which puts a damper on that potential benefit.

So neither can offer immediate relief, but both offer good options for fleets to plan for the next inevitable oil shock – which is why Range didn’t base its analysis solely on current prices (remember, we just had another shock in 2022, this nonsense happens all the time, maybe it’s time to stop using oil). But, the numbers in the paper for the Tesla Semi can be compared to numbers for other electric tractors already available today, which can in turn be compared to the costs of the eTrailer, for fleets so inclined to make that comparison.
